hobbies.name: Motorcycle Riding
hobbies.description: I have a deep passion for motorcycles—riding them, researching new models and technologies, and spending time maintaining my own. Whether it's tuning the engine, cleaning every detail, or upgrading parts, I find joy in every aspect of bike care. Sometimes, it's as simple as grabbing a coffee with a friend and chatting about bikes—sharing stories, discussing modifications, or dreaming about our next ride.

hobbies.name: Photography
hobbies.description: I've just recently started exploring photography and videography, and I'm still very much an amateur. I currently use a Canon 77D and an Insta360 Ace Pro. They may not be top-of-the-line gear, but they serve me well and have helped me learn a lot.

hobbies.name: Touring
hobbies.description: Sometimes, I spend my weekends in scenic places with sea or mountain views—perfect settings for a BBQ party with friends. Other times, it's just a quiet moment over a cup of coffee, enjoying the fresh air and good company. And of course, my motorcycle is always part of the journey—whether it's the ride that gets me there or the companion that makes the moment complete.

hobbies.name: PCMR
hobbies.description: It's not really about gaming for me—I genuinely enjoy searching for PC parts and learning how to assemble an entire system from scratch. The process of picking the right components, understanding how they work together, and building something functional and powerful is what excites me most.

hobbies.name: Gaming
hobbies.description: I'm part of the PC Master Race, so yeah—I mostly game on my rig. Sometimes it's just something simple to relax, like Solitaire or Minesweeper. Other times, I dive into more intense titles like Devil May Cry or Battlefield. I haven't been playing as much lately, but I still enjoy the thrill of a good challenge when I get the chance. Just like with coding, I always like to push myself.

skills.name: JS
skills.description: I've been using JavaScript since 2014, mostly self-taught. I was really fond of it back then—especially when I saw people doing magic-like things with jQuery, transforming entire websites into a whole new level of UI and UX. Then came the ECMAScript versions, and I've been following them closely ever since.

skills.name: TS
skills.description: I love JavaScript and have spent a lot of time understanding it. Through that journey, I've learned its pros and cons. From the perspective of a strict OOP learner back then, JavaScript had countless drawbacks for me. That's where TypeScript came in and helped solve many of those issues. It doesn't fix everything, but it addresses some major problems—and I really appreciate how Microsoft listens to developers to continuously improve and enhance it. Even now, I still use TypeScript every day.

skills.name: Angular
skills.description: My first-ever JavaScript framework was AngularJS. Before that, JavaScript was just a plain interpreted script to me. So when I first started using AngularJS, it felt like heaven—it introduced rules to follow and concepts to develop around. Then came Angular 2, and my heaven was upgraded with object-oriented programming-like features. Although I don't work with it as much as I used to, I still love the concept, its capabilities, and how well it can scale an application.

skills.name: React
skills.description: In 2017, I used ReactJS for the first time. It was still JavaScript, but I managed to grasp the concepts and understand the code flow. I also learned about state management and libraries like Redux and redux-observable (though I guess no one really uses that one anymore). Since then, I've expanded my skills—exploring React Native (I was once an Android developer too), diving into React functional components, and much more.

skills.name: NodeJS
skills.description: In the same year—2017—I learned NodeJS and explored how it handles workers, asynchronous operations, and non-blocking architecture. Later, I started working with frameworks like ExpressJS and Kraken. Eventually, I discovered NestJS, which felt like Angular for the backend—structured, scalable, and built with TypeScript, of course.

skills.name: GraphQL
skills.description: It's not going to replace REST APIs!
